title: Changes, Modifications, Adaptations of the Maternal Organism During Pregnancy
summary:
The chapter reviews how each body system adapts to pregnancy and what that means for exercise. These adaptations are described as necessary physiological responses, not pathological ones, and they are not uniform across women or across the pregnancy.

The cardiovascular, blood, respiratory and metabolic systems all change substantially: heart rate, blood volume, ventilation and energy needs rise, while weight gain targets depend on prepregnancy BMI. The musculoskeletal system shows ligament laxity, a shifted center of gravity, abdominal diastasis and altered gait. Emotional changes vary by trimester, and renal, digestive, skin, nervous, immune and reproductive systems also adapt. The chapter stresses that systems interact, so prenatal exercise is a multisystemic stimulus that should be individualized.
points: Cardiovascular changes begin around the fifth week of gestation and can continue up to a year after delivery.
Resting heart rate rises by 10-20 beats/min (up to 30%), and blood volume increases by 40-45% with red blood cells up 18-25%, causing physiological anemia of pregnancy.
Anemia is defined as hemoglobin below 11 g/100 ml; pregnancy also brings hypercoagulability.
Minute ventilation increases 30-40%, oxygen consumption rises 10%-20%, and the diaphragm rises about 4 cm when standing.
Basal metabolic rate increases 15%-20%, and energy needs rise by about 300 kcal/day from the second trimester.
Recommended total weight gain by prepregnancy BMI: under 18.5 is 12.5-18 kg, normal is 11.5-16 kg, overweight is 7-11.5 kg, and obese is 5-9 kg; first trimester gain is 0.5-2.0 kg for all.
Relaxin and progesterone increase ligament laxity, the center of gravity shifts, the rectus abdominis separates (diastasis), and gait speed, cadence and stride length fall, raising fall risk.
Emotional patterns differ by trimester: anxiety and tiredness in the first, more energy in the second, insomnia and fear of childbirth in the third.
Renal plasma flow and glomerular filtration rise about 50%, increasing urinary frequency and infection risk.
takeaways: Combine heart rate monitoring with the Borg scale or the Talk Test, and recalculate heart rate monthly.
Favor moderate aerobic exercise and avoid maximal or strenuous training.
Stay hydrated, eat frequent balanced meals, have a snack before training, and avoid training on an empty stomach or prolonged fasting.
Avoid high-impact exercise, bouncing, excessive stretching, and crunches or prolonged front planks; train balance, lumbopelvic stability and posture.
Practice slow deep breathing and avoid breath holding (Valsalva); exercise in cool, well-ventilated places with breathable clothing.
Include urination breaks, start pelvic floor work (adapted Kegel) from the first trimester, and keep moving to avoid sedentary behavior.
cautions: Avoid long periods lying on the back because of the risk of supine hypotension syndrome.
Avoid prolonged fasting, which can cause maternal hypoglycemia and ketosis that is harmful to the fetus.
Avoid sudden posture changes, quick turns and sudden movements, and watch for dizziness or exhaustion.
